findings.title: Test uses default EC key for all algorithms, masking wrong-size behavior for ES384/ES512
findings.body: The constructor generates a single key with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, which on most JDKs produces a P-256 key (32-byte components). `ECDSAAlgorithm.ES384` and `ES512` expect 48-byte and 66-byte components respectively, but the JDK's Signature returns ~32-byte r/s for a P-256 key regardless of the requested algorithm name. `asn1derToConcatenatedRS(sign, 96)` then pads the 32-byte components with leading zeros to 48 bytes, and the subsequent RS->DER->RS round-trip is consistent because the same padding is applied again. The test passes, but `asn1Des != sign` and the resulting signature cannot be verified against the data. Each `test*` method should generate a key with the matching curve (P-256 for ES256, P-384 for ES384, P-521 for ES512), e.g. via `ECGenParameterSpec` and `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` initialized appropriately.

findings.title: Test only verifies round-trip consistency, not absolute correctness of concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: The assertion `Assert.assertArrayEquals(rsConcat, rsConcat2)` only proves that `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` is idempotent over its own output, which is essentially a property of the decoder. A buggy `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` that, for example, swapped r and s, added a spurious leading zero, or used the wrong tag/byte order, could still satisfy this equality. The test should additionally assert `Assert.assertArrayEquals(sign, asn1Des)` and, more importantly, verify the produced signature against the data with the public key (`Signature.initVerify(...); signature.update(data); Assert.assertTrue(signature.verify(asn1Des));`). Without that, a real conversion bug would not be caught.

findings.title: Dead `ASN1Encoder.create().write(...)` calls in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: Lines 114-115 call `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger)` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger)` and then immediately discard the returned instances (no assignment, no `toByteArray()`). The encoders' internal `ByteArrayOutputStream`s accumulate the encoded bytes that are then thrown away. The actual return value is built only by the subsequent `ASN1Encoder.create().writeDerSeq(...)` call. The two lines are dead code that waste allocations and obscure intent; they should be deleted.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default JCA provider, not BouncyCastle
findings.body: The implementation does `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which on a stock JDK returns the SUN provider (for JKS) - not BouncyCastle. The contract on `CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider()` (documented as "BouncyCastle security provider") is violated, and any authz-client code path that uses this provider for BC-only algorithms (e.g. certain Signature/Cipher/KeyFactory lookups requested without an explicit provider name) will fail with `NoSuchAlgorithmException` or get a non-BC implementation. The authz-client explicitly advertises itself as a self-contained CryptoProvider, so this method should return a real BouncyCastleProvider (matching what the other CryptoProvider implementations do), or the doc/comment on the class should be updated to state that BC algorithms are unsupported and `getBouncyCastleProvider()` is intentionally a stub.

findings.title: Adding `int order()` as a non-default abstract method is a binary-incompatible API break
findings.body: `order()` is declared without a `default` body, so every external implementation of `CryptoProvider` (third-party SPIs registered via `META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider`) will fail to load with `NoSuchMethodError` / `AbstractMethodError` at `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` time. Before this PR such implementations would be the only ones on the classpath (no ordering needed); afterwards they are still detected by `ServiceLoader` and either shadow the bundled providers or get shadowed by them, but every call site that compiled against the old interface breaks at runtime. Either provide a sensible `default int order() { return 0; }` (or `Integer.MIN_VALUE`) so existing implementations keep working, or document this as an intentional breaking change and bump the module's major version. Without a default, downstream Keycloak extensions and forks will start crashing on startup.

findings.title: Tie-breaking by ServiceLoader iteration order is non-deterministic when orders are equal
findings.body: When two providers share the same `order()` value (e.g. `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return 200 here), `Comparator.reversed()` is stable, so the winner is whichever provider ServiceLoader happens to iterate first. JAR ordering on the classpath is not specified by the JLS, and tools/builds can produce different orders, so the chosen CryptoProvider can differ between environments with the same dependency set. This previously threw a clear error; now it silently picks an implementation. The log line also leaks a format string into `logger.debugf(builder)` (class names contain no `%` so it's safe today, but it should be `logger.debugf("%s", builder.toString())`). Either reject equal orders with an informative error, or sort by a secondary deterministic key (class name) and document the precedence.

findings.title: CryptoIntegration.init is called from create(Configuration) but not from create() / create(InputStream) entry points
findings.body: `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())` is added only to the `create(Configuration)` overload. Although `create()` and `create(InputStream)` both delegate to `create(Configuration)` and so transitively initialize the provider, the contract of `CryptoIntegration.init` is that callers invoke it explicitly with their own classloader, and double-checked init inside `init` records the *first* classloader it sees. Any caller that constructed an `AuthzClient` via a non-default classloader (e.g. inside an OSGi bundle, a JEE lib isolation, or an app-server deployment that also exposes `keycloak-authz-client`) will have the choice of CryptoProvider pinned to the AuthzClient class's loader, even though a more appropriate provider exists on their loader. The init should happen in every public `create(...)` overload, or be done once eagerly in a static initializer / `ServiceLoader` lookup that does not depend on which API the user calls first.
